Another engineer probed the binary and proposed this rule for "CLI contract and exact output formatting":

----- PROPOSED RULE -----
PROGRAM I/O CONTRACT (byte-exact, verified by hexdump)

1) ARGUMENT HANDLING
- Let argc be the raw process argument count (including argv[0]).
- if argc < 2  (i.e. no arguments after the program name, or even argc==0 via execve with an empty argv):
    write NOTHING to stdout, NOTHING to stderr, exit status 1.
- if argc >= 2: use argv[1] verbatim as the URL string. argv[2..] are read but never used and never affect
  output; exit status 0. (Confirmed with 2, 3, 51 and 1001 arguments.)
- argv[1] == "" (empty string) is a normal input, NOT the no-arg case: prints "0\n0\n0\n0\n0\n", exit 0.
  It does not fall through to a later non-empty argument.
- No option parsing whatsoever. "-h", "--help", "--version", "-v", "-", "--", "---" are treated as ordinary
  URL strings (e.g. "--help" -> "1\n0\n0\n0\n1\n--help\n").
- The argument is an ordinary NUL-terminated C string, so a NUL byte can never appear in the input; every other
  byte 0x01..0xFF is accepted verbatim (no validation, no transcoding, no locale/encoding sensitivity).
- Max testable argument length is the Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN limit of 131072 bytes: 131071-byte args work
  perfectly (exit 0, complete output); 131072+ is rejected by the kernel (E2BIG) before the program runs, so
  no program-side length limit is observable. No truncation, no crash at 131071 bytes.

2) STDOUT FORMAT  (this is the ENTIRE output; there is nothing else)
   line 1: is_valid_url(url)          -> exactly one byte '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30), then LF
   line 2: is_scheme_valid(scheme)    -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 3: is_host_valid(host)        -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 4: is_port_valid(port)        -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 5: N = path_segments.size()   -> plain unsigned decimal ASCII, no sign, no '+', no leading zeros
                                         (except the value 0 itself printed as "0"), no thousands separators,
                                         no padding, no spaces; then LF
   lines 6..5+N: each path segment, raw bytes exactly as stored, then LF.
- Bools use the default C++ numeric form (no boolalpha): never "true"/"false", never uppercase, never padded.
- Separator/terminator is always a single LF (0x0A). Never CR, never CRLF. No BOM. No leading/trailing spaces.
  A trailing LF is ALWAYS present after the last line (std::endl). Total output for argc>=2 therefore always
  ends with 0x0A and always contains at least 5 LFs.
- Exact byte count of stdout for argc>=2:
      total_bytes = 8 + (number of decimal digits in N) + 1 + sum over segments of (len(segment) + 1)
  Verified: 'http://example.com' -> 10 bytes; 'http://example.com/a/b/c' -> 16 bytes;
  1234 segments of length 3 -> 8 + 5 + 1234*4 = 4949 bytes (actual 4949).
- Segments are printed RAW and unescaped/undecoded. If a segment contains an LF byte, the output becomes
  ambiguous (a "segment" spans two output lines). Therefore line count == 5 + N only when no segment contains
  an LF. Example: $'http://ex.com/a\nb/c' -> "1\n1\n1\n0\n2\na\nb\nc\n" (6 physical lines, N=2; segment 1 is
  "a\nb", segment 2 is "c"). TAB (0x09), CR (0x0D), VT, FF, space (0x20), 0x7F and all high bytes 0x80..0xFF
  pass through byte-for-byte inside segments; there is no quoting, escaping, percent-decoding, or trimming.
- Empty segments are never printed (they are dropped before printing), so no output line among 6..5+N is ever
  a bare LF unless the segment itself literally contains an LF.
- A segment never contains '/' (0x2F).

3) STDERR
- Never written to, for any input. Verified 0 bytes of stderr across ~1800 probes: every single byte 0x01-0xFF
  as the whole argument, as a host character, and as a path character; 500 random 60-byte urandom strings;
  400 structured token-fuzz URLs; port values 2147483648, 4294967296, 99999999999999999999, -2147483649 and a
  5000-digit port (no std::stoi out_of_range escapes -> library catches it; no "terminate called ..." message,
  no SIGABRT/exit 134 ever observed).

4) EXIT STATUS
- 1  : argc < 2 (no output at all).
- 0  : every other case, for every input tested, including empty string, control bytes, invalid UTF-8,
       131071-byte arguments, 65526 path segments, and port overflow.
- 141 (SIGPIPE, 128+13): only when the reader closes the pipe early (e.g. `| head -1`) while the program still
  has lines to write. Output is flushed line-by-line (std::endl), so this is reachable for outputs of >= ~3
  lines; a 12-byte output typically finishes first and yields 0 (race).
- Writing to a failing stdout is silently ignored: `>/dev/full` gives exit 0 with empty stderr (stream error
  state is never checked). Closed stdout (`>&-`) also gives exit 0, silently.

5) NON-INFLUENCES (all verified)
- stdin is never read (piping data in or /dev/null changes nothing).
- Environment is irrelevant: `env -i`, LANG/LC_ALL/LC_NUMERIC = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, POSIX,
  invalid_LOCALE all give identical bytes; line 5 is never locale-grouped (12345 stays "12345").
- argv[0] value/path is irrelevant (renaming the binary changes nothing).
- Fully deterministic: 30 identical runs of a complex URL produce identical md5.
- The program itself emits LF only; the CR seen under a pty (`script`) is the terminal's ONLCR translation,
  not program output.

RUST-IMPLEMENTABLE PSEUDOCODE
  let args: Vec<OsString> = env::args_os().collect();      // args[0] is program name
  if args.len() < 2 { exit(1); }                            // nothing printed
  let url: &[u8] = args[1].as_bytes();
  let u = URL::parse(url);
  let mut out = Vec::new();
  out.extend(if URL::is_valid_url(url) {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  out.extend(if is_scheme_valid(u.scheme) {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  out.extend(if is_host_valid(u.host)     {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  out.extend(if is_port_valid(u.port)     {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  let segs = split_path(u.path);
  out.extend(format!("{}\n", segs.len()).as_bytes());       // usize, plain decimal
  for s in &segs { out.extend(s); out.push(b'\n'); }        // raw bytes
  stdout().write_all(&out) (ignore errors); exit(0);

They flagged these uncertainties:
  - Arguments longer than 131071 bytes cannot be delivered on Linux (MAX_ARG_STRLEN), so any program-internal length limit above that is untestable; nothing suggests one exists.
  - A NUL byte can never appear in argv, so segment content containing 0x00 is unreachable and untested.
  - Flush granularity was inferred from SIGPIPE behavior (exit 141 with `| head -1` for outputs of >= ~3 lines) rather than observed syscall-by-syscall (strace unavailable). For a 12-byte output the SIGPIPE outcome is a race (observed exit 0).
  - Maximum observed segment count is 65526 (limited by the 131071-byte argument cap); behavior of line 5 at values requiring >5 digits (e.g. 100000+) is extrapolated from 1..65526 all printing as plain decimal.
  - Whether the process would report a nonzero status on a write error is settled for /dev/full and closed fd (both exit 0), but other error modes (e.g. EIO mid-write) were not exercised.

YOUR LENS: **extremes-and-robustness**. Attack the rule specifically from that angle.

Your job is to BREAK IT. Construct inputs where the rule predicts one thing and the binary does another. Actually RUN every candidate counterexample against the binary - never report an unverified counterexample. Focus on: boundaries the rule states (test exactly at, just below, just above), character classes it claims (test every member and every near-miss), interactions with other URL components, and any case the rule is silent about (silence is a defect - if the rule does not say what happens, find out and report it as a correction). Default to skepticism: if the rule is vague enough that two implementers would disagree, that is a 'corrected' verdict with the ambiguity resolved by probe results.

Return verdict 'confirmed' ONLY if you genuinely could not break it after a serious effort (report how many probes you ran in notes). Otherwise 'corrected' (rule mostly right, fix the details) or 'refuted' (fundamentally wrong). Always fill correctedRule with the COMPLETE rule as it should read.

input.correctedRule:
PROGRAM I/O CONTRACT (byte-exact; corrected under an extremes/robustness lens, ~1900 probes)

1) ARGUMENT HANDLING
- Let argc be the raw process argument count (including argv[0]).
- if argc < 2: write NOTHING to stdout, NOTHING to stderr, exit status 1. This includes argc==0, now
  DIRECTLY VERIFIED via execve(path, {NULL}, environ): exit 1, 0 bytes stdout, 0 bytes stderr.
- if argc >= 2: use argv[1] verbatim as the URL string. argv[2..] are never used and never affect output.
  Verified with 2, 3, 51, 1001, 5000 and 20000 extra arguments — output identical every time.
- argv[1] == "" is a normal input, not the no-arg case: prints "0\n0\n0\n0\n0\n" (10 bytes), exit 0.
- No option parsing whatsoever. "-h" -> "1\n0\n0\n0\n1\n-h\n"; "--help" -> "1\n0\n0\n0\n1\n--help\n";
  "--version", "-v", "-", "--", "---", "-x" likewise treated as ordinary path strings.
- The argument is a NUL-terminated C string, so 0x00 can never appear in the input. Every byte 0x01..0xFF is
  accepted verbatim, in every position, with no validation, transcoding, trimming or locale sensitivity.
  Verified: all 255 single-byte arguments, and all 255 bytes repeated 131071 times (no crash, no stderr,
  every run exit 0 and under 300 ms).
- Length ceiling is the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 131072: a 131071-byte argv[1] works perfectly (exit 0,
  complete output, no truncation); 131072+ is rejected by execve with E2BIG before the program runs. No
  program-internal length limit is observable, and none above 131071 is testable on Linux.

2) STDOUT FORMAT (the entire output, under normal successful writes)
   line 1: is_valid_url(url)       -> exactly one byte '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30), then LF
   line 2: is_scheme_valid(scheme) -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 3: is_host_valid(host)     -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 4: is_port_valid(port)     -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 5: N = path_segments.size() -> plain unsigned decimal ASCII: no sign, no '+', no leading zeros
           (0 prints as "0"), no grouping, no padding; then LF
   lines 6..5+N: each path segment, raw bytes exactly as stored, then LF.
- Bools use default C++ numeric form (no boolalpha): never "true"/"false".
- Separator/terminator is always a single LF (0x0A). Never CR, never CRLF, no BOM, no leading/trailing spaces.
  (The CR seen under a pty is the terminal's ONLCR translation, not program output.)
- REACHABLE RANGE OF N: 0 <= N <= 65536. 65536 is attained by argv[1] = 'a' + ('/a' x 65535) = 131071 bytes
  (line 5 = "65536", 65540 lines, 131086 bytes). Because n one-byte segments need 2n-1 bytes, N can never
  exceed 65536, so line 5 is ALWAYS 1-5 digits; six-or-more-digit values are unreachable, not merely untested.
- Byte count when all writes succeed:
      total_bytes = 8 + digits(N) + 1 + SUM over segments of (len(segment) + 1)
  Verified: 'http://example.com' -> 10; 'http://example.com/a/b/c' -> 16; 1234 segments of length 3 -> 4949;
  65536 one-byte segments -> 131086. Validated automatically against 700 randomized/token-fuzz inputs with
  zero violations (also: lines 1-4 always exactly "0" or "1"; line 5 always plain decimal; always >= 5 lines;
  always LF-terminated; no segment ever contains '/' (0x2F)).
- Segments print RAW: no escaping, quoting, percent-decoding or trimming. TAB 0x09, LF 0x0A, VT 0x0B, FF 0x0C,
  CR 0x0D, SPACE 0x20, 0x7F and all high bytes 0x80..0xFF pass through byte-for-byte, including when a segment
  consists solely of such a byte. Nothing is trimmed at either end of argv[1] (leading/trailing SPACE, TAB, CR
  and LF are all preserved; beware shell $(...) which strips trailing newlines and can fake a trim).
- Empty segments are dropped and never printed, so line count == 5 + N whenever no segment contains LF.
  A segment that contains LF spans multiple physical output lines: $'http://ex.com/a\nb/c' ->
  "1\n1\n1\n0\n2\na\nb\nc\n" (8 physical lines, N=2). A segment that IS a single LF yields a bare-LF output
  line: $'http://ex.com/\n/a' -> 31 0a 31 0a 31 0a 30 0a 32 0a 0a 0a 61 0a.

3) FLUSH GRANULARITY (now observed, not inferred)
- std::cout is stdio-synced (stdio_sync_filebuf). Each output line is emitted as exactly one fwrite of the
  payload + one putc('\n') + one fflush(stdout) — i.e. one flush (one write syscall to a pipe/file) PER LINE,
  confirmed by LD_PRELOAD interposition of fwrite/putc/fflush (8 fflush(fd=1) for an 8-line output).
- fd 2 is opened/flushed by iostream static teardown but is NEVER written by the program.

4) STDERR
- For every input, with normal resource limits: 0 bytes. Verified across ~1900 probes: all 255 single bytes,
  all 255 bytes x131071, 31 pathological token repeats padded to 131071 bytes, 700 randomized/structured
  fuzz inputs, and port values 2147483647/2147483648/4294967296/999999999999/99999999999999999999/
  -2147483648/-2147483649 (std::stoi out_of_range is caught internally — no terminate, no abort).
- EXCEPTION (rule previously claimed "never, for any input"): allocation failure is NOT handled. Under
  `ulimit -v 6000` with a 3001-segment URL the process aborts with exit 134 and writes 45 bytes to stderr:
  "terminate called without an active exception". Under `ulimit -v 4000` the dynamic loader fails first
  (exit 127, 128 bytes on stderr, "error while loading shared libraries: libc.so.6").

5) EXIT STATUS  (corrected: the set is {0, 1, 134, 137, 141, 153, 127}, not {0, 1, 141})
- 1   : argc < 2 (no output at all).
- 0   : every input-driven case with normal limits and a working stdout — empty string, control bytes,
        invalid UTF-8, 131071-byte arguments, 65536 path segments, port overflow.
- 141 : SIGPIPE (128+13) when the pipe reader closes early. This is a pure RACE at every output size, not a
        function of a line threshold: measured 141 rates were 1/100 at 5 lines (10 bytes), 1/100 at 7 lines,
        6/100 at 8 lines, 36/60 at 25 lines, 36/40 at 205 lines, and 10/10 only from ~805 lines upward.
        So 141 is reachable for the MINIMUM-size output and is not guaranteed even for a 200-line output.
        (`prog | true` on outputs under the 64 KiB pipe capacity reliably gives 0: the writer finishes into
        the pipe buffer before the reader exits.)
- 153 : SIGXFSZ, when stdout is a regular file and RLIMIT_FSIZE is exceeded mid-output. Output is TRUNCATED
        and may end mid-segment on a non-LF byte (measured: 1024 bytes, last byte 0x61).
- 134 : SIGABRT from unhandled allocation failure (see section 4).
- 137 : SIGKILL from RLIMIT_CPU exhaustion (`ulimit -t 0`).
- 127 : loader failure before main (extreme RLIMIT_AS).

6) WRITE-ERROR BEHAVIOUR (corrected)
- The stream error state is never checked, so write failures never change the exit status by themselves:
  `>/dev/full` (ENOSPC) -> exit 0, empty stderr, for both small and 90 KB outputs; `>&-` (closed fd 1) ->
  exit 0; fd 1 opened O_RDONLY -> exit 0; SIGPIPE set to SIG_IGN by the parent (inherited across exec) ->
  EPIPE swallowed, exit 0.
- CONSEQUENCE the rule missed: because errors are swallowed, stdout can be SILENTLY TRUNCATED while the exit
  status stays 0 and stderr stays empty. With stdout an O_NONBLOCK pipe (EAGAIN mid-write): a single
  131071-byte segment yields 61450 of the expected 131082 bytes with last byte 0x63 (no trailing LF, only
  5 LFs); 16 x 8000-byte segments yield 60114 of 128027 bytes, last byte 0x61, 12 LFs instead of 21;
  65536 one-byte segments yield exactly 65536 of 131086 bytes. Therefore the guarantees "always ends with
  0x0A", "always contains at least 5 LFs", "line count == 5+N" and the byte-count formula hold ONLY when
  every write to stdout succeeds. They are guarantees about what the program EMITS, not about what a reader
  necessarily RECEIVES.

7) NON-INFLUENCES (all re-verified)
- stdin is never read and never consumed: `{ prog url >/dev/null; cat; } < file` still prints the whole file.
  `<&-` (closed stdin) changes nothing.
- Environment is irrelevant: env -i, LC_ALL/LANG/LC_NUMERIC = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8,
  de_DE.UTF-8, ja_JP.eucJP, invalid_X, POSIXLY_CORRECT=1, and a 100 KB environment variable all yield an
  identical md5. Line 5 is never locale-grouped.
- argv[0] is irrelevant: renamed binary, symlink, and argv[0]=="" (via perl exec) all yield identical bytes.
- cwd is irrelevant. Fully deterministic: 30 identical runs produce identical md5 (twice).

RUST-IMPLEMENTABLE PSEUDOCODE
  let args: Vec<OsString> = env::args_os().collect();       // args[0] is program name (may be absent)
  if args.len() < 2 { exit(1); }                            // nothing printed, nothing on stderr
  let url: &[u8] = args[1].as_bytes();                      // arbitrary bytes 0x01..0xFF, len <= 131071
  let u = URL::parse(url);
  let segs = split_path(&u.path);                           // 0 ..= 65536 segments, none empty, none has b'/'
  let mut w = stdout();
  let mut emit = |b: &[u8]| { let _ = w.write_all(b); let _ = w.write_all(b"\n"); let _ = w.flush(); };
  emit(if URL::is_valid_url(url) { b"1" } else { b"0" });    // one flush per line (std::endl)
  emit(if is_scheme_valid(&u.scheme) { b"1" } else { b"0" });
  emit(if is_host_valid(&u.host)     { b"1" } else { b"0" });
  emit(if is_port_valid(u.port)      { b"1" } else { b"0" });
  emit(segs.len().to_string().as_bytes());                  // plain decimal, 1..5 digits
  for s in &segs { emit(s); }                               // raw bytes
  exit(0);                                                  // all write/flush errors ignored
  // NB: leave SIGPIPE at its default disposition to reproduce exit 141; do not catch OOM (abort with the
  // C++ "terminate called without an active exception" message on stderr, exit 134) if bit-compatibility
  // under RLIMIT_AS matters.

APPROACH: ~1900 probes total — 255 single-byte args, 255 args of one byte repeated 131071 times (timing + stderr + exit watched), 31 pathological token repeats padded to the 131071-byte ceiling, a 700-input randomized/structured self-verifying fuzzer (perl) that machine-checked the byte-count formula, the 0/1-only bools, plain-decimal line 5, trailing LF, >=5 lines, and "no '/' in any segment" (0 violations), ~480 SIGPIPE race trials at 5/7/8/25/55/105/205/405/805/1005+ line outputs, plus purpose-built C harnesses (execve with empty argv for argc==0; a fork/pipe launcher with O_NONBLOCK stdout; an LD_PRELOAD stdio interposer).

WHAT SURVIVED: the whole normal-path format (lines 1-5, 0/1 bools, plain decimal, raw segments, trailing LF, byte-count formula), the argc<2 -> exit-1-silent contract (now verified for argc==0 too), byte-verbatim pass-through of all 255 possible bytes in all positions, no trimming anywhere, stoi overflow being caught internally, and every "non-influence" (stdin, env, locale, argv[0], cwd, determinism, huge argv counts).

WHAT BROKE (why 'corrected', not 'confirmed'):
1. Exit-status set is wrong. The rule enumerates {1, 0, 141}. I reproduced 153 (SIGXFSZ under RLIMIT_FSIZE, with truncated non-LF-terminated output), 134 (SIGABRT + 45 bytes of stderr, "terminate called without an active exception", under RLIMIT_AS=6000K) and 137 (SIGKILL under RLIMIT_CPU=0).
2. "STDERR never written to" is falsified by the 134 case — allocation failure is unhandled. The rule specifically boasted "no 'terminate called ...' message, no SIGABRT/exit 134 ever observed"; it is observable.
3. "Writing to a failing stdout is silently ignored -> exit 0" is right, but the rule failed to draw the consequence: silence + swallowed errors means stdout can be silently TRUNCATED with exit 0 and empty stderr. Two clean counterexamples with O_NONBLOCK stdout end on a non-LF byte (0x63, 0x61), breaking "always ends with 0x0A" and the byte-count formula. This closes their own flagged uncertainty about untested write-error modes: EAGAIN mid-write -> silent truncation, exit 0.
4. The SIGPIPE characterisation is wrong in both directions. It is NOT deterministic above ~3 lines (7-line output: 1/100; 205-line: 36/40) and it IS reachable at the minimum output size (5-line, 10-byte output: 1/100 gave 141). It is a pure scheduling race up to ~800 output lines.
5. Max N is 65536, not 65526 (arg 'a'+'/a'x65535 = exactly 131071 bytes). This also converts their "extrapolated for 100000+" uncertainty into a proof: line 5 can never exceed 5 digits.
6. Flush granularity was flagged as inferred; I observed it directly by LD_PRELOAD-interposing fwrite/putc/fflush — exactly one fwrite + one putc('\n') + one fflush(stdout) per line, and fd 2 is only fflush'd at teardown, never written.

HARNESS PITFALL worth flagging to whoever probes next: bash $(...) command substitution strips trailing newlines, which makes $'\n'-terminated arguments look as though the library trims whitespace. It does not — pass such args directly ($'...') and every byte survives.

Still genuinely untestable: argv[1] longer than 131071 bytes (kernel E2BIG), and NUL bytes inside argv (impossible).

- Length ceiling is the kernel's MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 131072: a 131071-byte argv[1] works perfectly (exit 0,
  complete output, no truncation); 131072+ is rejected by execve with E2BIG before the program runs. No
  program-internal length limit is observable, and none above 131071 is testable on Linux.

2) STDOUT FORMAT (the entire output, under normal successful writes)
   line 1: is_valid_url(url)        -> exactly one byte '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30), then LF
   line 2: is_scheme_valid(scheme)  -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 3: is_host_valid(host)      -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 4: is_port_valid(port)      -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 5: N = path_segments.size() -> plain unsigned decimal ASCII: no sign, no '+', no leading zeros
           (0 prints as "0"), no grouping, no padding; then LF
   lines 6..5+N: each path segment, raw bytes exactly as stored, then LF.
- Bools use default C++ numeric form (no boolalpha): never "true"/"false".
- Separator/terminator is always a single LF (0x0A). Never CR, never CRLF, no BOM, no leading/trailing spaces.
  (The CR seen under a pty is the terminal's ONLCR translation, not program output.)
- REACHABLE RANGE OF N: 0 <= N <= 65536. 65536 is attained by argv[1] = 'a' + ('/a' x 65535) = 131071 bytes
  (line 5 = "65536", 65540 lines, 131086 bytes). Because n one-byte segments need 2n-1 bytes, N can never
  exceed 65536, so line 5 is ALWAYS 1-5 digits; six-or-more-digit values are unreachable, not merely untested.
- Byte count when all writes succeed:
      total_bytes = 8 + digits(N) + 1 + SUM over segments of (len(segment) + 1)
  Verified: 'http://example.com' -> 10; 'http://example.com/a/b/c' -> 16; 1234 segments of length 3 -> 4949;
  65536 one-byte segments -> 131086. Machine-validated against 700 randomized/token-fuzz inputs with zero
  violations (also: lines 1-4 always exactly "0" or "1"; line 5 always plain decimal; always >= 5 lines;
  always LF-terminated; no segment ever contains '/' (0x2F)).
- Segments print RAW: no escaping, quoting, percent-decoding or trimming. TAB 0x09, LF 0x0A, VT 0x0B, FF 0x0C,
  CR 0x0D, SPACE 0x20, 0x7F and all high bytes 0x80..0xFF pass through byte-for-byte, including when a segment
  consists solely of such a byte. Nothing is trimmed at either end of argv[1] (leading/trailing SPACE, TAB, CR
  and LF are all preserved; beware shell $(...) which strips trailing newlines and can fake a trim).
- Empty segments are dropped and never printed, so line count == 5 + N whenever no segment contains LF.
  A segment containing LF spans multiple physical output lines: $'http://ex.com/a\nb/c' ->
  "1\n1\n1\n0\n2\na\nb\nc\n" (8 physical lines, N=2). A segment that IS a single LF yields a bare-LF output
  line: $'http://ex.com/\n/a' -> 31 0a 31 0a 31 0a 30 0a 32 0a 0a 0a 61 0a.

3) FLUSH GRANULARITY (now observed, not inferred)
- std::cout is stdio-synced (stdio_sync_filebuf). Each output line is emitted as exactly one fwrite of the
  payload + one putc('\n') + one fflush(stdout) — i.e. one flush (one write syscall to a pipe/file) PER LINE,
  confirmed by LD_PRELOAD interposition of fwrite/putc/fflush (8 fflush(fd=1) for an 8-line output).
- fd 2 is opened/flushed by iostream static teardown but is NEVER written by the program.

4) STDERR
- For every input, with normal resource limits: 0 bytes. Verified across ~1900 probes: all 255 single bytes,
  all 255 bytes x131071, 31 pathological token repeats padded to 131071 bytes, 700 randomized/structured fuzz
  inputs, and port values 2147483647 / 2147483648 / 4294967296 / 999999999999 / 99999999999999999999 /
  -2147483648 / -2147483649 (std::stoi out_of_range is caught internally — no terminate, no abort).
- EXCEPTION (rule previously claimed "never, for any input"): allocation failure is NOT handled. Under
  `ulimit -v 6000` with a 3001-segment URL the process aborts with exit 134 and writes 45 bytes to stderr:
  "terminate called without an active exception". Under `ulimit -v 4000` the dynamic loader fails first
  (exit 127, 128 bytes on stderr, "error while loading shared libraries: libc.so.6").

5) EXIT STATUS  (corrected: the set is {0, 1, 127, 134, 137, 141, 153}, not {0, 1, 141})
- 1   : argc < 2 (no output at all).
- 0   : every input-driven case with normal limits and a working stdout — empty string, control bytes,
        invalid UTF-8, 131071-byte arguments, 65536 path segments, port overflow.
- 141 : SIGPIPE (128+13) when the pipe reader closes early. This is a pure RACE at every output size, not a
        function of a line threshold: measured 141 rates were 1/100 at 5 lines (10 bytes), 1/100 at 7 lines,
        6/100 at 8 lines, 36/60 at 25 lines, 36/40 at 205 lines, and 10/10 only from ~805 lines upward. So 141
        is reachable for the MINIMUM-size output and is not guaranteed even for a 200-line output.
        (`prog | true` on outputs under the 64 KiB pipe capacity reliably gives 0: the writer finishes into the
        pipe buffer before the reader exits.)
- 153 : SIGXFSZ, when stdout is a regular file and RLIMIT_FSIZE is exceeded mid-output. Output is TRUNCATED and
        may end mid-segment on a non-LF byte (measured: 1024 bytes, last byte 0x61).
- 134 : SIGABRT from unhandled allocation failure (see section 4).
- 137 : SIGKILL from RLIMIT_CPU exhaustion (`ulimit -t 0`).
- 127 : loader failure before main (extreme RLIMIT_AS).

6) WRITE-ERROR BEHAVIOUR (corrected)
- The stream error state is never checked, so write failures never change the exit status by themselves:
  `>/dev/full` (ENOSPC) -> exit 0, empty stderr, for both small and 90 KB outputs; `>&-` (closed fd 1) ->
  exit 0; fd 1 opened O_RDONLY -> exit 0; SIGPIPE set to SIG_IGN by the parent (inherited across exec) ->
  EPIPE swallowed, exit 0.
- CONSEQUENCE the rule missed: because errors are swallowed, stdout can be SILENTLY TRUNCATED while the exit
  status stays 0 and stderr stays empty. With stdout an O_NONBLOCK pipe (EAGAIN mid-write): a single
  131071-byte segment yields 61450 of the expected 131082 bytes with last byte 0x63 (no trailing LF, only
  5 LFs); 16 x 8000-byte segments yield 60114 of 128027 bytes, last byte 0x61, 12 LFs instead of 21;
  65536 one-byte segments yield exactly 65536 of 131086 bytes. Therefore "always ends with 0x0A", "always
  contains at least 5 LFs", "line count == 5+N" and the byte-count formula hold ONLY when every write to
  stdout succeeds. They are guarantees about what the program EMITS, not about what a reader RECEIVES.

7) NON-INFLUENCES (all re-verified)
- stdin is never read and never consumed: `{ prog url >/dev/null; cat; } < file` still prints the whole file.
  `<&-` (closed stdin) changes nothing.
- Environment is irrelevant: env -i, LC_ALL/LANG/LC_NUMERIC = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8,
  de_DE.UTF-8, ja_JP.eucJP, invalid_X, POSIXLY_CORRECT=1, and a 100 KB environment variable all yield an
  identical md5. Line 5 is never locale-grouped.
- argv[0] is irrelevant: renamed binary, symlink, and argv[0]=="" (via perl exec) all yield identical bytes.
- cwd is irrelevant. Fully deterministic: 30 identical runs produce identical md5 (twice).

RUST-IMPLEMENTABLE PSEUDOCODE
  let args: Vec<OsString> = env::args_os().collect();       // args[0] is program name (may be absent)
  if args.len() < 2 { exit(1); }                            // nothing printed, nothing on stderr
  let url: &[u8] = args[1].as_bytes();                      // arbitrary bytes 0x01..0xFF, len <= 131071
  let u = URL::parse(url);
  let segs = split_path(&u.path);                           // 0 ..= 65536 segments, none empty, none has b'/'
  let mut w = stdout();
  let mut emit = |b: &[u8]| { let _ = w.write_all(b); let _ = w.write_all(b"\n"); let _ = w.flush(); };
  emit(if URL::is_valid_url(url) { b"1" } else { b"0" });    // one flush per line (std::endl)
  emit(if is_scheme_valid(&u.scheme) { b"1" } else { b"0" });
  emit(if is_host_valid(&u.host)     { b"1" } else { b"0" });
  emit(if is_port_valid(u.port)      { b"1" } else { b"0" });
  emit(segs.len().to_string().as_bytes());                  // plain decimal, 1..5 digits
  for s in &segs { emit(s); }                               // raw bytes
  exit(0);                                                  // all write/flush errors ignored
  // NB: leave SIGPIPE at its default disposition to reproduce exit 141; do not catch OOM (abort with the C++
  // "terminate called without an active exception" message on stderr, exit 134) if bit-compatibility under
  // RLIMIT_AS matters.

APPROACH: ~1900 probes total — 255 single-byte args; 255 args of one byte repeated 131071 times (timing + stderr + exit watched); 31 pathological token repeats ('://', ':', '@', '?', '#', '%', '%2', '[]', './', '../', ':/', 'http://', ...) padded to the 131071-byte ceiling; a 700-input randomized/structured perl fuzzer that machine-checked the byte-count formula, the 0/1-only bools, plain-decimal line 5, trailing LF, >=5 lines and "no '/' in any segment" (0 violations); ~480 SIGPIPE race trials at 5/7/8/25/55/105/205/405/805/1005+ line outputs; plus purpose-built C harnesses (execve with empty argv for argc==0; a fork/pipe launcher with O_NONBLOCK stdout; an LD_PRELOAD stdio interposer).

WHAT SURVIVED: the whole normal-path format (lines 1-5, 0/1 bools, plain decimal, raw segments, trailing LF, byte-count formula), the argc<2 -> exit-1-silent contract (now verified for argc==0 too), byte-verbatim pass-through of all 255 possible bytes in all positions, no trimming anywhere, stoi overflow caught internally, and every "non-influence" (stdin, env, locale, argv[0], cwd, determinism, huge argv counts).

WHAT BROKE (why 'corrected', not 'confirmed'):
1. The exit-status set is wrong. The rule enumerates {1, 0, 141}. I reproduced 153 (SIGXFSZ under RLIMIT_FSIZE, with truncated non-LF-terminated output), 134 (SIGABRT + 45 bytes of stderr, "terminate called without an active exception", under RLIMIT_AS=6000K), 137 (SIGKILL under RLIMIT_CPU=0) and 127 (loader failure).
2. "STDERR never written to" is falsified by the 134 case — allocation failure is unhandled. The rule specifically boasted "no 'terminate called ...' message, no SIGABRT/exit 134 ever observed"; it is observable.
3. "Writing to a failing stdout is silently ignored -> exit 0" is right, but the rule failed to draw the consequence: swallowed errors mean stdout can be silently TRUNCATED with exit 0 and empty stderr. Two clean counterexamples with O_NONBLOCK stdout end on a non-LF byte (0x63, 0x61), breaking "always ends with 0x0A" and the byte-count formula. This closes their own flagged uncertainty about untested write-error modes: EAGAIN mid-write -> silent truncation, exit 0.
4. The SIGPIPE characterisation is wrong in both directions. It is NOT reliable above ~3 lines (7-line output: 1/100; 205-line: 36/40) and it IS reachable at the minimum output size (5-line, 10-byte output: 1/100 gave 141). It is a pure scheduling race up to ~800 output lines.
5. Max N is 65536, not 65526 (arg 'a' + '/a'x65535 = exactly 131071 bytes). This also converts their "extrapolated for 100000+" uncertainty into a proof: line 5 can never exceed 5 digits, since n one-byte segments need 2n-1 <= 131071 bytes.
6. Flush granularity was flagged as inferred; I observed it directly by LD_PRELOAD-interposing fwrite/putc/fflush — exactly one fwrite + one putc('\n') + one fflush(stdout) per line, and fd 2 is only fflush'd at teardown, never written.

HARNESS PITFALL worth flagging to whoever probes next: bash $(...) command substitution strips trailing newlines, which makes $'\n'-terminated arguments look as though the library trims whitespace. It does not — pass such args directly ($'...') and every byte survives. My first pass hit this and briefly "found" that a lone LF is trimmed; it is not (arg $'\n' gives 1 0 0 0 1 with a segment consisting of one LF byte: 31 0a 30 0a 30 0a 30 0a 31 0a 0a 0a).
